answers.question: I haven't run for two weeks. Do I have to start again from the beginning? And is the 5K in four weeks still realistic?
answers.answer:
No, you don't start again from the beginning. Sixteen days off costs a beginner some comfort, not the base you built. Monday repeats the 2 minute runs you already know, and Wednesday moves on to 3 minute runs.

Finishing the Corrowmore Harvest 5K on Sun Nov 15 is realistic. Running the whole way is a stretch. You have four weeks including race week, and you haven't yet run longer than 2 minutes at a time.

Treat the whole-way goal as a target, not a promise. If you can run about 20 minutes without stopping by Sun Nov 8, going the whole way at a slow pace is a fair aim. If you can't, we plan race day as long run pieces with short walk breaks, and you still run most of it.

new.analysis:
## What the two missed weeks change

You ran none of the three planned sessions in the week of Oct 12 – 18, after a week with no runs the week before. That came with your mum's hospital stay and a lot of driving, so the gap makes sense. I'm glad she is home.

The plan therefore restarts at a level you have already handled. Before the break you were running 16 to 18 minutes in total, in 2 minute pieces, with no pain. A short break barely dents that, but the first session back is where legs and lungs check in, so it should feel easy.

## Why no speed work, even this close to the race

Three weeks after this one is race week, which would normally mean race-pace work. For you, race pace is simply a slow, steady run, and you have never held one longer than 2 minutes. Speed sessions would add risk without getting you closer to the finish.

So the hard work in these weeks is longer continuous running, and all of it stays easy. Each week the run pieces should grow: 3 minutes now, 4 to 5 minutes next week, and 8 to 10 minutes in the week of Nov 2 – 8, with one longer run near 20 minutes. Race week is short and easy so you arrive fresh.

## Keeping the load sensible

Short sleep and high stress make the same run feel harder, and they slow recovery. That is why I'm keeping three runs with real rest days between them and adding nothing else, including no extra running on the dog walks. Longer pieces are the only thing changing, and pace stays slow so that the extra minutes don't also become extra effort.

If a week goes wrong again, tell me. A missed session is easy to plan around, but a missed fortnight is harder to fix with four weeks to go.
